messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: silly integral question
parts:
I'm writing up a doc and have confused myself about computing
posterior predictive densities on the log scale.

I know for new data y', observed data y, and parameters theta that
the posterior predictive density is defined by

p(y' | y) = INTEGRAL_Theta p(y' | theta) p(theta | y) d.theta.

But I (think I) want the log posterior density,

log p(y' | y) = log INTEGRAL_Theta p(y' | theta) p(theta | y) d.theta.

But instead, what I wind up with if I define

log_p <- log p(y' | theta)

in a Stan program will be this average:

1/M SUM_{m in 1:M} log p(y' | theta[m])

where theta[m] is the m-th posterior draw for theta. So
that corresponds to this integral:

INTEGRAL_Theta (log p(y' | theta)) p(theta | y) d.theta.

which can't be the same given that log doesn't even distribute
through addition.

So I'm OK with the whole posterior of log p(y' | y), but the posterior
mean of that isn't the mean of the posterior of p(y' | y).

So how do I actually compute the posterior log density? Is
it OK to just work with the expectation of the posterior log
density rather than the log of the expectation of the posterior density?

The immediate application is that I want to compare models based
on the log density on a held-out data set.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] silly integral question
parts:
You can bound the log expectation by the expectation of the log using Jensen’s inequality,
but the bound may not be all that tight. Interestingly enough, this discrepancy is a large
motivation behind WAIC — see http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf,
especially section 3.4, for how WAIC uses the expectation of the log to estimate the log
of the expectation.

messages.author: 49e107cb0f8a3d27
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] silly integral question
parts:
To directly answer the question, you would have to exponentiate log posterior densities to weight the likelihood terms p(y’ | theta) with p(theta | y), then take the mean, and then take the log. This comes up a lot, e.g., I am/Andrew is doing this when calculating importance weights during GMO. To do log(sum(exp))s in a numerically reasonable manner, you should take the max of the logs, subtract by that max, and then do log(sum(exp))) on that difference.

Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] silly integral question
parts:
Thanks.

I'd thought about factoring p = p[1] * p[2] * ... * p[N],
and then estimating each term separately and then log-sum-exp-ing.
I was sort of hoping there'd be a better solution, because even
that's going to be prone to underflow to 0 or overflow to 1 (the
former being a much bigger problem here, obviously).

I'm down with log_sum_exp --- I just went over it in Andrew's class,
in fact :-)

- Bob

P.S. One of the cool things Rob Zinkov was telling me about Hakaru is
that it expresses model in the natural domain, but works in the log
domain, so * -> + and + -> log_sum_exp implicitly.
